function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you prepare everything you’ll need—but because my execution sandbox doesn’t have internet access or permission to manipulate your private Git‑repository, I can’t actually **clone** the repo, write files inside it, or make commits/pushes for you.  
What *can* happen here is that I analyze the public source tree (if you paste it) or simply assume typical Node.js project layout, and then give you ready‑to‑copy templates for:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Container definition for the Node.js app |
| `k8s/deploy.yaml`, `k8s/service.yaml` | Deployment & Service manifests |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub/GitHub Packages |

Once you copy those files into the appropriate locations in your local checkout, just run the usual `git add … && git commit ... && git push origin main`.

Below are fully fleshed out examples that match a standard “Hello World” Express server (`app.js`) found in most starter projects. Feel free to tweak paths, ports, image names, etc., to fit your exact setup.

---

### 1️⃣ Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Python runtime as parent image
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

# Set workdir
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies first – cache layer reuse
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy rest of the source
COPY . .

# Build step (optional)
# RUN npm run build    # Uncomment if you have a build script

# Final minimal image
FROM node:20-alpine

ENV NODE_ENV production
EXPOSE 3000          # Change to whatever port your app uses

WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app .
CMD ["node","app.js"]
```

> **Why two stages?**  
> The multi‑stage build keeps the final image lean—just the compiled assets + runtime, nothing else.

If your repo already contains a Dockerfile, replace its contents with the snippet above (or merge accordingly).

---

### 2️⃣ Kubernetes Manifests

Create a folder called `k8s/` at the root of the repo and put the following two files there.

#### 2.1 `deploy.yaml`
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3                     # Adjust replica count as needed
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/<your-github-username>/nodejs-welcome:{{ .Values.imageTag }}
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000       # Same as EXPOSE in Dockerfile
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "3000"
---
```

#### 2.2 `service.yaml`
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # Switch to NodePort/ClusterIP if preferred
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                   # External port exposed by the cluster
    targetPort: 3000           # Matches container's listening port
```

> **Tip:** If you’re deploying to GKE/AWS EKS/etc., adjust `type:` and annotations accordingly.

---

### 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow

Place this under `.github/workflows/`. Name it anything descriptive, e.g., `build-and-publish.yml`.

```yaml
name: Build & Publish

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build_and_publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write     # Needed for GHCR publishing
      id-token: write     # For OIDC auth (recommended)

    steps:
    - name: Checkout Repo
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up QEMU
      uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-docker-${{ hashFiles('**/*.lock') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-docker-

    - name: Build and Push Image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        push: true
        platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64

    - name: Deploy to K8s (Optional)
      if: success()
      uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v2
      with:
        kubeconfig-value: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
      # Add further deploy steps (kubectl apply ...) after setting context
```

> **Key points**
>
> * Uses the built‑in `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` for authentication against GHCR.  
> * Builds multi‑arch images (`amd64`,`arm64`).  
> * You may want to store the resulting SHA/tag somewhere (e.g., update Helm values).  

Feel free to extend the job with lint checks, unit tests, or integration tests before building.

---

## How to Apply These Files Locally

Assuming you’ve cloned the repo locally:

```bash
cd ~/path/to/nodejs-welcome
mkdir -p k8s
cp <generated-dockerfile-path> Dockerfile
cp <generated-k8s-deploy-path> k8s/deploy.yaml
cp <generated-k8s-service-path> k8s/service.yaml
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cp <generated-gh-actions-path> .github/workflows/build-and-publish.yml
```

Stage, commit, and push:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/* .github/workflows/*
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8S manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Once pushed, the new GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on subsequent pushes to `main`, building and publishing your Docker image, while the Kubernetes manifests let you spin up the app wherever you prefer.
